title: Is my property an asset or a liability? Traders vs investors
excerpt: Property makes money through monthly rent or a gain on sale. Sean explains why a property that drains your account is a liability, and how tax shapes the trader's game.

qa.context: People make money from property in two ways: keeping units that earn rent, or buying and selling for a gain. Many first-time buyers stretch for a dream house, assuming any property is an asset.
qa.question: What makes a property an asset rather than a liability, and how do traders and investors differ?
qa.quote: assets are things that will bring money into your account every month
qa.answer: Following Rich Dad Poor Dad, Sean counts a property as an asset only if it puts money into your account each month; one that takes money out is a liability, which is why a dream home makes a poor first property. Investors buy and keep for rent; traders buy and sell for capital gains, and must play by the tax rules.

reasons.title: Small surpluses add up
reasons.body: A RM500,000 apartment on a 30-year loan costs about RM1,500 a month including maintenance; if it rents for RM1,800, you keep about RM300. Several such units build a monthly income.

reasons.title: Declared rent helps you borrow
reasons.body: Rental income you declare to the tax department counts as income, which can support further loans.

reasons.title: Traders live by the RPGT rules
reasons.body: When RPGT was waived after the 2008 crisis, traders flipped freely. By 2017, selling a home within a year meant 30% tax on the gain, and none after five years for residential property.

actions: Work out whether each property adds to or drains your monthly cash flow.
Avoid making a cash-draining dream home your first purchase.
Declare rental income so it counts toward future loans.
Check the current RPGT rates and your holding period before planning to sell.
Keep receipts for renovations, which can reduce the taxable gain.
qa.caveat: The RPGT rates are as Sean stated them in 2017 and have changed since; check the current rules before selling. Commercial property was taxed differently.

sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's English captions for this August 2017 video, which draws on Robert Kiyosaki's Rich Dad Poor Dad. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. His remarks on agents' commission rates are left out.
